subject: Gasoline is up 31%, core inflation is 1.8%
bodyMarkdown:
Statistics Canada said yesterday that inflation held at 3.1 per cent in October, and if you are renewing a mortgage or sitting on a variable rate, the number that matters to you is buried underneath that one. Strip out energy and prices rose 2.0 per cent, which is exactly where the Bank of Canada wants them.

## The gas pump is doing all the work

The headline matched September and came in a notch under the 3.2 per cent economists polled by Reuters had pencilled in. Month over month it was 0.2 per cent seasonally adjusted. Gasoline is up 30.9 per cent from a year ago, faster than September's 27.8 per cent, and Statistics Canada attributes part of that to a **base-year effect**, meaning the month being compared against was unusually cheap rather than this month being unusually expensive. Pump prices in October 2025 were low because oil markets were worried about oversupply, and the consumer carbon levy came off in April 2025. Both of those soft comparisons are now sitting in the denominator. Energy overall ran about 21.8 per cent. Clothing jumped 3.4 per cent in the month, the largest monthly move since September 2019, and groceries picked up as well.

## What the Bank's own core measures say

The Bank of Canada does not set policy off the headline. It watches **CPI-trim**, which drops the most extreme price moves in each direction before averaging what is left, and that came in at 1.8 per cent, down from 1.9. CPI-median held at 2.0 per cent. CPI-common ticked up to 2.5 from 2.4. Two of those three sit at or below target. This is awkward, because the Bank raised its policy rate 25 basis points to 2.50 per cent on October 28, its first increase since July 2023, and the Globe and Mail reported that it suggested more might be needed to contain an oil-price shock. An oil shock that has not leaked into anything else is not the sort of inflation a central bank fixes by making mortgages dearer.

## Markets cut the December odds

Traders repriced quickly. The Globe and Mail reported that the implied probability of a hike at the December 9 meeting fell to 38 per cent from 54 per cent before the release. The two-year yield dropped roughly four basis points to about 3.31 per cent, and the ten-year slipped about five to around 3.80 per cent. The loonie did what a dovish print tends to do and touched its weakest level against the US dollar since April 2025, near C$1.4297, which the Globe called a 19-month low. Economists split on what comes next. CIBC's Andrew Grantham said the tame report, softer gasoline and signs of a weakening labour market mean the Bank need not rush, and he still calls for a hold. RBC's Abbey Xu kept a 25 basis point December hike as her base case and said the report does not materially change her outlook.

## The takeaway

If you have a renewal coming in the next few months, December 9 looks closer to a coin flip than it did a week ago, and I would not lock a rate on the assumption that another hike is on the way. Keep an eye on oil, because the gasoline base effect falls out of the year-over-year figure early next year even if pump prices never move. The labour market is worth more of your attention than the CPI print right now, since Grantham's case for holding rests on jobs rather than prices. I will be reading the Bank's December statement for whether it is still calling this an oil shock.
